Welcome Back and the Scale of Things

Welcome back, team! It is always a little tough to get back into the swing of things after a nice long three-day weekend, but we have a lot of exciting ground to cover today.

To start us off on a cheerful note, let’s talk about the MOSFET replicas you all built last week. We had some fantastic submissions, and as promised, the winning groups get a prize. And what better prize for learning about computer chips than... actual potato chips! (Get it? Devices on chips? I know, I know, the dad jokes are free.) But honestly, just by being here and learning nanoscience, every single one of you is a winner in my book.

Now, let’s get our heads in the game with a quick warm-up exercise. Last week, you made these macro-scale replicas of transistors. Some of you managed to make your replicas as small as 1\text{ cm} wide, and a few even got down to 5\text{ mm}. But a state-of-the-art nanoscale transistor (a MOSFET) is about 50\text{ nanometers} wide.

I want you to think about this: how many of those actual nanotransistors could fit across the width of your 1\text{ cm} replica? And how many could fit inside the total area?

Crunching the Numbers: 1D Scaling

Let’s walk through the math together. We are trying to figure out how many times smaller the actual nanotransistor is compared to our replica. To do this, we just divide the big number by the small number.

First, let’s get everything into the same units—meters. Our replica width is 1\text{ cm}, which is 10^{-2}\text{ meters}. Our actual nanotransistor width is 50\text{ nm}. Since "nano" means 10^{-9}, we can write this as 50 \times 10^{-9}\text{ meters}. To make the math a little cleaner, let’s adjust that decimal point: \begin{align*} 50 \times 10^{-9}\text{ m} &= (5 \times 10^1) \times 10^{-9}\text{ m} \\ &= 5 \times 10^{-8}\text{ m} \end{align*}

Now, we divide the big width by the small width: \begin{align*} \frac{\text{Big}}{\text{Small}} &= \frac{10^{-2}\text{ m}}{5 \times 10^{-8}\text{ m}} \end{align*}

To solve this without breaking a sweat, we can separate the numbers out front from the powers of 10. Remember that there is an invisible "1" in front of our 10^{-2}: \begin{align*} \frac{1 \times 10^{-2}}{5 \times 10^{-8}} &= \left(\frac{1}{5}\right) \times \left(\frac{10^{-2}}{10^{-8}}\right) \end{align*}

We know that \frac{1}{5} is 0.2. For the exponents, when we divide, we subtract the bottom exponent from the top one (-2 - (-8) = 6): \begin{align*} 0.2 \times 10^6 \end{align*}

Having a decimal out front is a little annoying, so let’s borrow a power of 10 to turn that 0.2 into a 2: \begin{align*} 0.2 \times 10^6 &= (2 \times 10^{-1}) \times 10^6 \\ &= 2 \times 10^5 \end{align*}

That is 200,000. You could fit two hundred thousand nanotransistors across the width of your 1\text{ cm} replica! In science, we often care more about the order of magnitude (the power of 10) than the exact number out front. So, we can say the nanotransistor is about 5\text{ orders of magnitude} (10^5) smaller than the replica.

Crunching the Numbers: 2D Area

What about the area? If we can fit 200,000 transistors across the width, and we assume the device is roughly square, we can fit another 200,000 along the length. To find the total number of transistors that fit in the area, we just square our 1D ratio!

\begin{align*} \text{Area Ratio} &= (\text{Width Ratio})^2 \\ &= (2 \times 10^5)^2 \\ &= 2^2 \times (10^5)^2 \\ &= 4 \times 10^{10} \end{align*}

That is 40\text{ billion} transistors fitting into the area of a single 1\text{ cm} square. That is 10\text{ orders of magnitude} difference!

A quick note on precision: what if your replica was 5\text{ mm} instead of 1\text{ cm}? Your leading number would change (you might get 1 \times 10^{10} instead of 4 \times 10^{10}), meaning you are off by a factor of 4. Is that a big deal? In some fields, like administering medicine, yes! But when we are talking about the sheer scale of nanotechnology, being off by a factor of 4 doesn’t really matter when the order of magnitude (10^{10}) is so massive. Always check your exponents first—that is where the real story is.

How Do We Make Things This Small?

So, here is the million-dollar (or perhaps billion-dollar) question: How on earth do we actually mass-produce these teeny, tiny nanoscale MOSFETs?

I heard some great, creative guesses from the class today. Nanoscale saws? Tiny lasers? Microscopic robots acting as a mini-factory? Those all sound like awesome science fiction, and maybe one day we’ll have nanobots doing our manufacturing. But the reality is a bit different.

Let’s look at where we started.

This is the very first transistor ever made, back in 1947. It is centimeter-scale, completely handmade, and honestly, it’s a work of art. You can see the key components: the emitter (source), the collector (drain), and the base (gate). But there is no way we can build 40\text{ billion} of these by hand to fit on a modern computer chip.

The answer to our mass-production problem is a process called photolithography.

Let’s break that buzzword down. It comes from Greek:

  • Photo = Light (like photosynthesis or photography)

  • Litho = Stone (or in our case, a mold or template)

  • Graphy = Writing or making a pattern

Put it all together, and photolithography means using light to pattern devices on a substrate (like silicon). Instead of building a tiny device piece by piece with microscopic tweezers, we use light to carve out millions of devices all at once.

The Clean Room: Keeping the Bugs Out

Before we look at the steps of photolithography, we need to talk about where this happens. You can’t just do this on your kitchen counter. You need a clean room.

Why do we need such a pristine environment? Think about the scale we just calculated. Our transistors are 50\text{ nm} wide. A single particle of dust or pollen floating in the air is on the micrometer scale—that is thousands of times larger than our device! If a dust particle lands on your silicon wafer during manufacturing, it’s like a massive boulder crushing a city. Your device is cooked.

Major companies like Intel, TSMC, and Samsung spend billions of dollars building massive fabrication facilities (called "fabs"). Inside, the workers wear full-body outfits called "bunny suits."

Your first instinct might be that these suits protect the humans from nasty chemicals. While there are dangerous chemicals involved, the main purpose of the bunny suit is actually to protect the devices from the humans! We humans are pretty gross on a microscopic level. We are constantly shedding dead skin cells, hair, and oils. The bunny suit keeps our organic debris from raining down and destroying the nanoscale patterns we are trying to build.

Step-by-Step: The Photolithography Playbook

Alright, let’s get into the actual process. How do we use light to carve a nanoscale pattern? We are going to walk through a simplified version of the steps.

Here is our starting point. We have a substrate (like a piece of silicon) coated with a thin film of material we want to pattern (let’s say it’s gold). Our goal is to carve away almost all of that gold, leaving just a tiny, specific rectangular strip behind.

Step 1: Spin Coat the Photoresist

First, we coat the entire surface with a special chemical called a photoresist. Think of this like a protective layer of paint, but with a superpower: it is highly sensitive to ultraviolet (UV) light. When UV light hits it, the chemical structure of the photoresist changes.

Step 2: Mask Alignment

Next, we bring in our blueprint, which we call a photomask. This is basically a stencil. It has areas that are completely transparent (letting light pass through) and areas that are opaque (blocking light). We carefully align this mask right above our photoresist-coated wafer.

Step 3: UV Exposure

Now we turn on the UV light! The light shines down, passing through the clear parts of the mask and hitting the photoresist. The dark part of the mask casts a shadow, protecting a specific area of the photoresist from the light. The areas that get hit by the UV light undergo a chemical reaction, changing their properties.

Step 4: Develop

We then wash the wafer in a special chemical bath called a developer. Because the UV light changed the chemical properties of the exposed photoresist, the developer easily dissolves it away. The part that was hiding in the shadow of the mask stays firmly in place. Now we have a physical pattern made of photoresist sitting on top of our gold film.

Step 5: Etch

This is where we actually carve our device. We expose the wafer to an etchant—this could be a strong acid or a beam of accelerated ions. The etchant eats away all the exposed gold film. However, the leftover photoresist acts like a shield, protecting the gold directly underneath it from being destroyed.

Step 6: Photoresist Removal

Finally, we don’t need our photoresist shield anymore. We use a different solvent to strip it away, and voila! We are left with our beautifully patterned, nanoscale strip of gold on the silicon substrate.

Layering Up and Trying It Yourself

Of course, a real transistor is much more complex than a single rectangular strip. To build a functional modern chip, engineers repeat this entire photolithography process over and over again—sometimes dozens of times—stacking different patterned layers of metals, insulators, and semiconductors on top of each other to build intricate 3D structures.

To help you get an intuitive feel for this, I handed out envelopes at the start of class containing a piece of blue "sun paper" and a transparency sheet. This is your take-home photolithography lab!

The blue paper is your substrate coated with a UV-sensitive photoresist. The transparency is your photomask. If you draw a dark pattern on the transparency, place it over the blue paper, and leave it out in the sun for 10 to 20 minutes, the UV rays from the sun will react with the exposed paper. Once it changes color, you act as the "developer" by dunking it in water to wash away the exposed chemicals, leaving your pattern behind.

Give it a try at home, and we will talk about how your "fabrication runs" went in our next class!
